neighbours.label: ' all' used as an intensifying adverb before a particle or phrase (all by herself, all together, all along, all too well, all over again), as against 'all' as a quantifier over a noun or pronoun
fire: After the movers left, my grandmother unpacked the boxes all by herself.
The new manager scrapped the old schedule all together last spring.
Looking back, the quiet clerk had been the thief all along.
Parents of teenagers know that silence all too well.
When the hard drive failed, the author had to write the chapter all over again.
The toddler insisted on tying his shoes all by himself this morning.
Honestly, the detective suspected the butler all along.
Small shops see that kind of theft all too often these days.
quiet: After the movers left, my grandmother unpacked all the boxes in an hour.
The new manager scrapped all five of the old schedules last spring.
Looking back, the clerks all agreed that the thief was quiet.
Parents of teenagers know all the tricks for ending a silence.
When the hard drive failed, the author lost all his notes for the chapter.
The toddler insisted on tying all his shoes himself this morning.
Honestly, the detective suspected all three butlers at once.
Small shops see thefts on all days of the week these days.
